title: Model Architectures
scopeHtml: Scope: decoder-only vs encoder-only vs encoder-decoder, Mixture-of-Experts, state-space/hybrid models, reasoning models and test-time compute, multimodal architectures, small vs large models, distillation. (Attention/KV math lives in the Transformer chunk; serving cost in C2; training stages in the training chunk.)

questions.promptHtml: Explain the three transformer architecture families (encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder). What is the real difference, and give one production use for each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the difference is the attention mask and training objective, not "different networks", and whether you pick the right tool instead of defaulting to a chat LLM.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The blocks are the same; what changes is the attention mask and the objective. Encoder-only, like BERT, uses bidirectional attention and masked-token prediction, so it makes great representations for classification, NER and embeddings but cannot generate. Decoder-only, like GPT or Llama, uses a causal mask and next-token prediction, so it generates and is what chat LLMs use. Encoder-decoder, like T5 or the original Transformer, encodes the input bidirectionally and a decoder cross-attends to it, which suits translation and summarization. For a classifier at 5k QPS I would reach for an encoder; for open-ended generation, a decoder."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
First principles: a transformer block is attention + FFN. Attention computes, for each position, a weighted mix of other positions. Which positions it may look at is controlled by a mask on the score matrix.

Encoder-only (bidirectional)   Decoder-only (causal)      Enc-dec
 every token sees every token   token i sees tokens <= i   encoder: full visibility
 x x x x                        x . . .                    decoder: causal self-attn
 x x x x                        x x . .                      + cross-attn to encoder states
 x x x x                        x x x .
 x x x x                        x x x x
Family Mask Objective Output Typical models
Encoder-only bidirectional masked LM (predict masked tokens) a vector per token BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, many embedding models
Decoder-only causal next-token prediction next-token distribution GPT family, Llama, Mistral, Claude-class chat models
Encoder-decoder enc: full; dec: causal + cross-attn span corruption / seq2seq generated sequence conditioned on input T5, BART, Whisper (audio encoder, text decoder)

Runtime behavior: an encoder processes the whole input in one parallel pass and is done; cost is one forward pass. A decoder generates token by token, so latency scales with output length and it needs a KV cache. Encoder-decoder pays the encoder once, then decodes with cross-attention over fixed encoder states.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(the mask is the whole difference)

import torch

n = 5
causal = torch.tril(torch.ones(n, n, dtype=torch.bool))   # decoder self-attention
full = torch.ones(n, n, dtype=torch.bool)                  # encoder self-attention
scores = torch.randn(n, n)
causal_scores = scores.masked_fill(~causal, float("-inf")).softmax(-1)
full_scores = scores.masked_fill(~full, float("-inf")).softmax(-1)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "BERT is old so useless." Encoders remain the cost-efficient choice for classification, reranking and embeddings.
  • Claiming decoders cannot "understand" context to the right. They can, they just encode each position causally; late tokens see everything before them.
  • Calling Whisper or T5 "encoder-only"; they are encoder-decoder.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can an encoder-only model not generate text naturally? → It was trained to fill masked positions given both sides, so there is no left-to-right factorization of the sequence probability to sample from.
  2. Which family do embedding models usually come from? → Historically bidirectional encoders; recent strong embedding models are often fine-tuned decoder-only LLMs with pooling (verify per model), so the line is blurring.
  3. Can a decoder-only model do the job of an encoder-decoder? → Yes: put the source in the prompt as a prefix. You pay full self-attention over source + target and lose the bidirectional view of the source, but you gain one simple architecture and scale.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names BERT/GPT/T5 and their tasks. Senior: frames it as mask + objective, links to cost profile (one pass vs autoregressive loop with KV cache), and chooses by task and latency budget rather than by hype.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams routing every intent-classification call through a chat LLM paid 50-100x more per request than a fine-tuned small encoder that scored the same on their eval.

questions.promptHtml: Why did decoder-only models win for general-purpose LLMs, when encoder-decoder looks like a more natural fit for "input to output" tasks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the scaling and simplicity arguments rather than repeating "GPT is popular".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Three reasons. Every training token is a supervised signal in next-token prediction, so data efficiency per token is high and the objective scales cleanly. One stack handles every task as 'continue this text', so prompting, in-context learning and instruction tuning all fit with no task-specific heads. And inference infrastructure is simpler: one KV cache, one decode loop. Encoder-decoder isn't worse in principle at small scale; decoder-only just got the most scaling investment and tooling."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Objective: causal LM gives a loss at every position of every sequence. Masked LM only gets loss on ~15% of tokens (BERT's rate), so it extracts less signal per forward pass.
  • Unification: translation, QA, coding, classification can all be phrased as prompt + continuation. This made few-shot and instruction tuning natural.
  • Engineering: one model type means one set of kernels (FlashAttention, paged KV cache), one quantization story, one serving stack. Encoder-decoder needs cross-attention caches and two sub-models to batch.
  • Prefix caching: in decoder-only, a shared system prompt prefix is reusable across requests via KV cache; the causal mask makes prefix states independent of what follows.
  • Caveat: at matched compute some studies found encoder-decoder or prefix-LM competitive on seq2seq tasks; the dominance is partly path dependence plus scaling investment, not a proven theoretical win. Present it that way.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: (none needed)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming decoder-only is strictly superior; the evidence is mixed and ecosystem effects matter.
  • Forgetting the 15% masked-token efficiency point.
  • Saying "causal attention is a limitation for understanding", without noting that models can still be made strong encoders by fine-tuning.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a prefix-LM? → Bidirectional attention over the prompt, causal over the output; one stack that gets some encoder-decoder benefit.
  2. Does causal masking hurt retrieval/embedding quality? → Mean/last-token pooling over causal states works but needs contrastive fine-tuning; some work re-enables bidirectional attention for embedding use.
  3. Why does a shared prefix cache work only with causal masking? → Because each token's states depend only on earlier tokens, so a cached prefix is valid whatever follows. With bidirectional attention, changing the suffix changes the prefix states.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "GPT proved it works." Senior: objective efficiency, task unification, serving simplicity, honest caveat that it is partly ecosystem momentum.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Serving stacks (paged KV, prefix caching, speculative decoding) were built decoder-first, so an encoder-decoder model often loses on tooling even when its architecture suits the task.

questions.promptHtml: A model card says "47B total parameters, 13B active". What does that mean, and what does it imply for compute, memory and quality?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common MoE trap: confusing compute savings with memory savings.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "In a Mixture-of-Experts model, each FFN layer is replaced by many expert FFNs plus a router, and each token is sent to only a few of them. Total parameters are everything that must exist in memory; active parameters are what a single token actually touches. So per-token FLOPs look like a 13B dense model, but I still need memory for all 47B weights. MoE saves compute, not memory. Quality tends to land between a 13B dense model and a 47B dense model, usually closer to the latter on knowledge-heavy tasks."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Take Mixtral 8x7B (Mistral, arXiv 2401.04088; 8 experts per layer, top-2 routing, Apache 2.0). Using its published dims (d_model 4096, FFN hidden 14336, 32 layers, GQA with 8 KV heads; verify against the model config), I can reproduce the headline numbers:

One expert FFN (SwiGLU: 3 matrices)     = 3 * 4096 * 14336        = 176.2M
8 experts * 32 layers                   = 176.2M * 8 * 32         = 45.1B
Attention per layer: q,o 2*4096*4096 + k,v 2*4096*1024 = 41.9M; *32 = 1.34B
Embeddings + output (32000 vocab)       = 2 * 32000 * 4096        = 0.26B
Total                                   ~ 46.7B
Active (2 of 8 experts)                 = 11.3B + 1.34B + 0.26B   ~ 12.9B

Implications:

  • Compute per token ~ 2 * active params FLOPs (~26 GFLOPs here), like a ~13B dense model.
  • Memory: all 46.7B weights must be resident: ~93 GB in bf16, ~47 GB in 8-bit, ~23 GB in 4-bit. That is why a "13B-speed" model does not fit on a 24 GB card at bf16.
  • Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, and at batch sizes large enough every expert gets hit, so you read nearly all weights per step anyway. Latency gains over a dense 47B shrink at high batch.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
d, ffn, L, E, k, kv_dim, vocab = 4096, 14336, 32, 8, 2, 1024, 32000
expert = 3 * d * ffn
attn = 2 * d * d + 2 * d * kv_dim
emb = 2 * vocab * d
total = L * (E * expert + attn) + emb
active = L * (k * expert + attn) + emb
print(f"total {total/1e9:.1f}B active {active/1e9:.1f}B")

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "MoE reduces memory." It does not; it usually raises it versus a dense model of equal active size.
  • Reading "8x7B" as 56B. Attention, embeddings and norms are shared, so the total is 46.7B.
  • Assuming latency equals a 13B dense model regardless of batch size.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is quality better than a 13B dense? → More total capacity (knowledge stored across experts) with the same per-token compute.
  2. Is "active parameters" the right size to compare against a dense model? → Only for FLOPs. For memory use total; for quality comparisons use evals.
  3. Name another MoE and its ratio. → DeepSeek-V3 is reported at 671B total / 37B active (verify against its technical report); many newer open models follow an "NNB-AMB" naming scheme.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "only some parameters run." Senior: does the arithmetic, states memory vs compute vs bandwidth, and notes batch size changes the picture.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team sized GPUs for "13B active" and discovered at load time that 93 GB of weights did not fit on the single 80 GB card they had budgeted.

questions.promptHtml: How does routing work in a Mixture-of-Experts layer, and how do training recipes stop the router from collapsing onto a few experts?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests mechanism-level understanding beyond the buzzword, and whether you know load imbalance is a quality and a systems problem.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A small linear router scores each token against every expert, we keep the top-k scores, softmax them into weights, and the layer output is the weighted sum of those experts' outputs. Left alone, the router self-reinforces: experts that get more tokens train faster, get chosen more, and the rest starve. So training adds an auxiliary load-balancing loss that penalizes uneven token distribution, plus an expert capacity limit that drops or reroutes overflow tokens. Some newer recipes, like DeepSeek-V3's, balance with per-expert bias terms instead of a loss, to avoid hurting the main objective."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism for a token vector x (d_model), E experts, top-k:

logits = x @ W_r                (E,)
top    = topk(logits, k)        indices
w      = softmax(logits[top])   weights sum to 1  (Mixtral-style: softmax over the selected k)
y      = sum_i w_i * Expert_i(x)

Switch Transformer (arXiv 2101.03961) used k=1 with an auxiliary loss proportional to N * sum_i f_i * P_i, where f_i is the fraction of tokens dispatched to expert i and P_i is the mean router probability for expert i; minimized by uniform routing. Their coefficient alpha was 1e-2 after a sweep from 1e-1 to 1e-5. Capacity per expert = (tokens per batch / experts) * capacity_factor; tokens over capacity are dropped and pass through on the residual path.

Failure modes: (1) router collapse early in training; (2) token dropping hurting quality when capacity is tight; (3) load balancing loss that is too strong hurting the language-modeling loss; (4) at inference there is no capacity limit by default in many implementations, but imbalance still hurts GPU utilization (see the serving question).

Variants: expert-choice routing (experts pick tokens, perfectly balanced but awkward for autoregressive decoding); shared experts always on plus routed experts (used in DeepSeek-style designs; verify per model).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def moe_forward(x, router, experts, k=2):
    # x: (T, d); router: Linear(d, E); experts: list of FFN modules
    logits = router(x)                         # (T, E)
    topv, topi = logits.topk(k, dim=-1)        # (T, k)
    w = F.softmax(topv, dim=-1)                # normalize over selected experts only
    out = torch.zeros_like(x)
    for slot in range(k):
        for e, ex in enumerate(experts):
            mask = topi[:, slot] == e
            if mask.any():
                out[mask] += w[mask, slot, None] * ex(x[mask])
    return out

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying experts specialize by human-readable topic. Mixtral's authors report routing correlates more with syntax/position than domain (verify in the paper's analysis section).
  • Treating balance as only a training concern; at serving time hot experts become bottleneck GPUs.
  • Applying softmax over all E logits and then top-k without renormalizing, which changes output scale vs the trained model.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens to tokens dropped by the capacity limit? → They skip the expert and flow through the residual connection unchanged, a silent quality loss.
  2. Why top-2 and not top-1? → More expressive combination and more stable gradients to the router; top-1 (Switch) cuts compute and communication.
  3. How would you detect collapse in a run? → Log per-expert token fraction and router entropy per layer; a few experts holding most mass or entropy falling toward zero is the signal.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "router picks top-2 experts." Senior: writes the dispatch math, names the aux loss and capacity factor, and ties imbalance to both quality and GPU utilization.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Fine-tuning an MoE on a narrow domain without freezing the router pushed most tokens to 2 experts, degraded general ability, and made one GPU the straggler.

questions.promptHtml: What is a "reasoning model" and what is test-time (inference-time) compute? How does it differ from just prompting a normal model with "think step by step"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know reasoning models are trained differently, and who understand the cost/latency consequences, from those who treat them as a prompt trick.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A reasoning model is trained, usually with reinforcement learning on verifiable outcomes like math answers and unit tests, to produce a long chain of thought before the final answer, and to use that scratchpad to explore, check and backtrack. Test-time compute means I spend more tokens at inference to get better answers, so quality scales with thinking length, not only model size. 'Think step by step' on a normal model is a prompt that elicits a short chain; a reasoning model has learned the behavior, so it is more reliable on hard problems, but it is slower and costs more because the thinking tokens are generated and typically billed."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Mechanism: an autoregressive model gets a fixed amount of computation per token. Emitting more tokens lets it carry intermediate state in text, an effectively deeper computation. Training rewards chains that end in a correct, checkable answer, so the model learns useful strategies (verification, trying alternatives). DeepSeek-R1 (arXiv 2501.12948) showed this with RL (GRPO, which estimates the baseline from a group of sampled answers instead of a learned value network); R1-Zero used RL without SFT, and the full R1 added cold-start SFT data to fix readability and language mixing.
  • Architecturally it is usually the same decoder-only (or MoE) transformer. The difference is the training stage and the inference behavior, not a new block type.
  • Scaling knobs: sampling many answers and voting or using a verifier (parallel), versus one longer chain (sequential). Providers expose a thinking budget or effort setting; names differ per vendor (verify current API).
  • Costs: reasoning tokens occupy context, add latency (TTFT to first visible token is long), and are billed as output tokens by most providers (verify). Streaming UX has to handle a long silent phase.
  • Where it helps: math, code, multi-step planning, constraint satisfaction. Where it does not: simple extraction, classification, retrieval-grounded lookups, and tasks where latency is user-facing.
Normal model:    prompt -> [short answer]                      ~100 output tokens
Reasoning model: prompt -> [thinking ... 4,000 tokens] -> answer ~100 visible tokens
cost/latency scale with total generated tokens, not visible ones

sections.label: Code
sections.html: (none; see the cost scenario for budgeting)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying reasoning models are "bigger". Often the same size, trained differently.
  • Applying few-shot CoT prompts or "think step by step" to a reasoning model; vendors generally advise simpler prompts (verify per provider).
  • Treating the visible chain of thought as a faithful explanation of the model's actual computation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does more thinking help? → More serial computation and the ability to verify and backtrack in text.
  2. Does quality scale forever with thinking tokens? → No, returns diminish and overthinking on easy problems wastes tokens and can hurt.
  3. How is training different? → Verifiable rewards (answer correctness, test pass) instead of only human preference; no per-step human labels needed in R1-style recipes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it thinks before answering." Senior: RL on verifiable rewards, same architecture, cost/latency/billing impact, and a routing policy that sends only hard queries to the reasoning tier.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Swapping a reasoning model into a high-volume support flow multiplied p95 latency by roughly 10x and the token bill by several x with no measurable quality gain on simple tickets.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech must classify incoming customer emails into 40 intents. Volume is 3M emails/day (peak ~120 QPS), average 250 tokens, p95 latency budget 150 ms, one 16 GB GPU class per node. They have 60k labeled examples; current macro-F1 is 0.84 with a TF-IDF + logistic regression baseline. A teammate proposes calling a hosted frontier chat model with a 12-example few-shot prompt ("it will be 0.9 out of the box"). Estimated prompt: 1,800 tokens in, 10 out. Illustrative price: $2.50 per 1M input tokens.
questions.promptHtml: Which architecture and model family do you pick, and how do you justify it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use the biggest LLM because it is smartest." Ignores cost (1,800 tokens x 3M = 5.4B input tokens/day, about $13.5k/day at the stated price), latency, and that labeled data exists.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How stable is the label set (new intents monthly changes the answer)? Are errors asymmetric (fraud vs spam)? Can data leave our VPC? Are non-English emails present? What is the acceptable F1 gain per dollar?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I would ship the baseline now and run the comparison in shadow mode.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A fine-tuned encoder (DeBERTa/ModernBERT-class base, ~100-400M params) beats the baseline and approaches or exceeds few-shot LLM at 60k labels. (b) The hosted LLM wins only if labels shift often. (c) A small decoder fine-tuned with a classification head is a middle path.
  4. How I'd verify each: Same held-out set of 5k emails with the baseline, the encoder, the few-shot LLM, and a small fine-tuned decoder; compare macro-F1 per class, p95 latency under 120 QPS, and cost per 1k emails. Run a latency benchmark on the actual GPU.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable; the decision is driven by task shape: closed label set + plenty of labels + tight latency favors a bidirectional encoder with a classification head (one forward pass, no generation loop).
  6. Fix: Fine-tune the encoder; ship with a confidence threshold that sends low-confidence emails (say the lowest 8%) to the LLM as a fallback. Encoder inference of ~250 tokens is single-digit to low tens of ms on a GPU (verify by benchmark).
  7. Prevention: Drift monitor on prediction distribution, weekly relabeled audit sample, a "new intent" bucket that triggers review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not start with the LLM: ~$13.5k/day vs a one-time training cost plus a few GPU nodes. I would not drop the LLM entirely: it is the right tool for the long tail and for bootstrapping labels.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Intents now change weekly → Hybrid: LLM labels new data, periodically distill into the encoder; or use embeddings + small head for fast retraining.
  • Emails arrive in 12 languages → Multilingual encoder (XLM-R-class) or multilingual LLM; re-run the eval per language.
  • Need explanations for the compliance team → Keep the LLM on a sampled audit path; encoder predictions alone have no rationale.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team launched with a frontier LLM classifier, hit the finance review in month two, and replaced 90% of traffic with a fine-tuned encoder in a week. The LLM stayed only as the fallback for low-confidence cases.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks by hype, no numbers.
  • Hire: picks an encoder with reasoning and does the token cost math.
  • Strong hire: adds the confidence-gated hybrid, benchmark plan, drift monitoring and per-language evaluation.

questions.promptHtml: How does a vision-language model like LLaVA let a text LLM "see" an image? Walk through the architecture and what is trained when.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand multimodality as tokens in the same sequence, which drives cost, latency and failure modes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A vision encoder, typically a CLIP ViT, turns the image into a grid of patch embeddings. A small projector, a linear layer or MLP, maps those into the LLM's embedding space so they look like token embeddings. They get concatenated with the text tokens and the decoder processes everything as one sequence. Training is usually staged: first train only the projector to align vision and language, then fine-tune the projector and LLM on visual instruction data. Image tokens consume context and compute like text tokens do."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
LLaVA (arXiv 2304.08485): frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder, trainable projection matrix; stage 1 aligns features training only the projector on image-caption pairs, stage 2 fine-tunes projector + LLM on instruction data generated with text-only GPT-4 from captions and boxes. LLaVA-1.5 (arXiv 2310.03744) swapped the linear projection for an MLP and used a 336px CLIP encoder, a cheap and effective improvement.

image 336x336 --ViT-L/14--> (336/14)^2 = 24*24 = 576 patch vectors (dim 1024)
            --MLP projector--> 576 vectors (dim = LLM d_model, e.g. 4096)
text "What is in the image?" --tokenizer+embed--> ~7 vectors
LLM input sequence = [576 image tokens][7 text tokens]  -> causal decoder -> answer

Design axes:

  • Connector: linear/MLP (keeps all patches, many tokens), or a resampler/Q-Former (compresses to a fixed small number of queries, fewer tokens but information loss), or cross-attention layers inside the LLM (Flamingo-style).
  • Resolution: higher resolution or tiling gives more patches, so better OCR/detail but quadratically more tokens in attention. Many systems tile a large image into crops plus a thumbnail.
  • Natively multimodal models trained from scratch on interleaved tokens exist; vendors rarely publish the details, so avoid specifics for closed models (verify).

Consequences: a 576-token image is like a 400-word prompt of cost; a 4-tile high-res image can be ~2,900 tokens; vision models fail on tiny text, counting, spatial relations and charts when the resolution or patching loses detail.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch.nn as nn

class Projector(nn.Module):          # LLaVA-1.5 style two-layer MLP
    def __init__(self, vit_dim=1024, llm_dim=4096):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(vit_dim, llm_dim), nn.GELU(),
                                 nn.Linear(llm_dim, llm_dim))
    def forward(self, patches):      # (B, 576, 1024) -> (B, 576, 4096)
        return self.net(patches)
# inputs_embeds = torch.cat([image_embeds, text_embeds], dim=1)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the LLM receives pixels or a text caption. It receives projected embeddings.
  • Forgetting image tokens count toward the context window and the bill.
  • Assuming OCR-grade accuracy at low resolution.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why freeze the vision encoder in stage 1? → Cheap alignment: only the small projector must learn the mapping, protecting both pretrained components.
  2. Why do VLMs miscount objects? → Patch embeddings are pooled semantic features; precise counting needs fine spatial info the encoder and training data underweight.
  3. How would you cut image token cost 4x? → Lower resolution, a compressing connector (resampler), or pooling patches; evaluate OCR and detail tasks since those degrade first.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "CLIP plus LLM." Senior: shapes and token counts, staged training, connector trade-offs, and the cost/latency/accuracy impact of resolution.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A document-QA service switched to high-resolution tiling for OCR accuracy and its per-request tokens tripled, which showed up as both latency and bill.

questions.promptHtml: What are state-space models like Mamba, how do they differ from attention, and why do production teams build hybrids?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the attention alternatives at concept level and can reason about KV-cache memory versus fixed-size state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A state-space layer compresses the history into a fixed-size state that it updates per token, like a learned recurrence, so compute grows linearly with sequence length and decode memory is constant, with no growing KV cache. Mamba makes the state update input-dependent, 'selective', so it can choose what to remember. The weakness is that a fixed state is lossy, so exact recall of arbitrary earlier tokens, like in-context retrieval, is weaker than attention. Hybrids such as Jamba interleave a few attention layers with many Mamba layers to get most of the memory savings and keep the recall."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Attention keeps all past keys and values: memory grows O(n) per layer, work O(n^2) in prefill. An SSM layer keeps a state h_t = A_t h_{t-1} + B_t x_t, y_t = C_t h_t, with size independent of n. Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) made A, B, C depend on x_t; training uses a parallel scan so it still trains efficiently on GPUs.

KV vs state, for a Llama-style 8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, bf16):

KV per token = 2 (K,V) * 32 layers * 8 heads * 128 * 2 bytes = 131,072 B = 128 KiB
128k context = 128k * 128 KiB = 16 GiB per sequence
SSM state: fixed (order of tens of MB per sequence, model dependent; verify), independent of length

Jamba (AI21, arXiv 2403.19887): interleaved Transformer and Mamba layers, reported 1:7 attention-to-Mamba ratio in the chosen config, with MoE on some layers; their ablations reported pure Mamba struggling with in-context learning that the hybrid retained (as summarized by secondary sources; verify in the paper).

When it matters: long-context serving where KV memory limits concurrency; streaming. When not: tasks needing precise retrieval from long context, and where the ecosystem (kernels, quantization, fine-tuning tooling) matters more than architecture elegance.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(toy recurrence showing constant state)

import numpy as np

def ssm_scan(x, A, B, C):
    # x: (T, d_in); state h: (d_state,) fixed size regardless of T
    h = np.zeros(A.shape[0]); ys = []
    for xt in x:
        h = A @ h + B @ xt
        ys.append(C @ h)
    return np.stack(ys)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying SSMs have "infinite context." The state is fixed size, so information is lossy.
  • Claiming hybrids replace transformers wholesale; most frontier deployments remain attention-based.
  • Ignoring the tooling gap (fewer optimized kernels, serving support, fine-tune recipes).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is attention good at recall? → Every past token is addressable via its key; an exact lookup is possible.
  2. Does a hybrid still have a KV cache? → Yes, but only for the attention layers, so with a 1:7 ratio it is about 1/8 the size of an all-attention stack of the same depth (same head config).
  3. How would you evaluate whether to adopt one? → Needle/recall tests at your length, throughput at your concurrency, and quality on your task evals; not the vendor's headline benchmark.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Mamba is faster than transformers." Senior: constant-state vs growing KV math, the recall trade-off, why hybrids exist, and the ecosystem caveat.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams serving 128k-token documents found KV memory capped concurrency at a handful of sequences per GPU, which is the exact pain hybrids target.

questions.promptHtml: When would you choose a small model (1-8B) over a large one (70B+ or a frontier API)? What do you give up?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical judgment: cost, latency and privacy vs capability, with evidence.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I pick the smallest model that passes my eval at the required reliability. Small models win on cost, latency, on-device or private deployment, and fine-tuning ease. They lose on broad knowledge, multi-step reasoning, instruction-following on messy prompts, and robustness to out-of-distribution inputs. Narrow, well-defined tasks like extraction, classification and routing are where a tuned small model often matches a big one; open-ended reasoning and long, ambiguous tasks still favor large models."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Cost and speed: decode is memory-bandwidth-bound. A 8B model at bf16 reads about 16 GB of weights per step; a 70B reads about 140 GB, so tokens/sec per GPU differs by roughly 8-9x before batching effects. Weights also set how many GPUs you need.
  • Capability: knowledge capacity grows with parameters; small models hallucinate more on long-tail facts. Reasoning and instruction-following improve with scale and data quality; modern small models trained on lots of tokens have closed much of the gap on narrow tasks (check current model cards).
  • Customization: LoRA/full fine-tune of a 7B is cheap; domain-specific tuning can beat a general large model on that domain.
  • Hybrid patterns: small model first, escalate on low confidence; small model for drafting (speculative decoding, see the serving chunk); small distilled student for the hot path.
  • Decision rule: build the eval first, run 3 sizes, plot quality vs cost, choose the knee of the curve.
Need Lean small Lean large
Closed task, labeled data yes
Edge/offline/privacy yes
Open-ended reasoning, coding agents yes
Long-tail world knowledge yes

sections.label: Code
sections.html: (none)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing size by parameter count instead of an eval on your data.
  • Forgetting total cost includes engineering time to host and tune small models.
  • Assuming a small model with a long prompt will behave like a big one; instruction following degrades faster.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a smaller model faster at decode? → Fewer bytes of weights streamed per token.
  2. What does fine-tuning buy a small model? → Format reliability and domain skill, not new broad knowledge.
  3. How do you decide when to escalate to the big model? → Calibrated confidence, schema-validation failures, or a cheap classifier on query difficulty; measure escalation rate and blended cost.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "small is cheaper, big is better." Senior: eval-first, bandwidth arithmetic, escalation design.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 7B tuned for extraction hit 97% of the large model's accuracy at about a tenth of the serving cost, but failed badly on the 3% unusual documents, which needed the escalation path.

questions.contextHtml: You serve a dense 13B model (bf16) on single 40 GB GPUs at 6 QPS with p95 of 1.2 s. Product wants better quality, and a vendor suggests a 47B-total / 13B-active MoE ("same speed as what you have now"). Traffic will grow 10x to 60 QPS next quarter. GPUs available: 80 GB class, 8 per node. Average request: 1,500 prompt tokens, 300 output tokens. KV per token for this MoE is 128 KiB (GQA, bf16; assume the same as the dense model for simplicity). Staging test on one 80 GB GPU: model fails to load.
questions.promptHtml: Why did it fail, what do you propose, and what do you tell the PM about "same speed"?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Quantize until it fits" without computing anything, or "MoE is 13B so it must fit".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is quality required at bf16 or is 8-bit/4-bit allowed (eval it)? Concurrency target and max context? Is single-node deployment required? What is the latency SLO at 60 QPS?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the dense 13B serving; do not promise the MoE date. Run the MoE only in an offline eval.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Weights alone are 47B x 2 B = 94 GB > 80 GB, so load fails; (b) KV cache needs additional memory; (c) a config/dtype error. Only (a) needs math to confirm.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute weights size; check nvidia-smi and the engine's load log for the allocation that fails; compute KV budget.
  5. Root cause: MoE saves FLOPs, not memory: 94 GB of resident weights. Even at 8-bit, 47 GB leaves only 33 GB minus overhead for KV on one 80 GB GPU.
  6. Fix: KV per request = 1,800 tokens x 128 KiB = 225 MiB. Short-term: shard across 2 GPUs (tensor parallel and/or expert parallel): 94 GB weights / 2 = 47 GB each, leaving ~25 GB each after overhead, for roughly 100+ concurrent sequences' KV per pair (25 GB x 2 / 225 MiB, approx 220 before fragmentation; plan lower). Concurrency need: at 60 QPS and, say, 8 s average request time (assumption: 300 output tokens at ~40 tok/s), Little's law gives 60 x 8 = 480 concurrent sequences, so about 480 x 225 MiB = 105 GB of KV, which means several GPU pairs. Long term: benchmark 8-bit weights, FP8 KV cache, and replicas; reserve capacity by measured, not estimated, throughput.
  7. Prevention: Capacity model in a spreadsheet (weights, KV, concurrency, headroom) reviewed before model swaps; load test with realistic length distributions.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not quantize to 4-bit blindly: MoE routers and quantization interact, so re-run evals. I would not trust "same speed": at larger batches nearly all experts are active so memory reads approach the full 94 GB per step, and cross-GPU communication adds latency.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Only 40 GB GPUs are available → Needs at least 3 per copy at bf16 (94/40) with a TP degree such as 4; or 4-bit weights (~24 GB) on one, with an eval for quality loss.
  • Mostly short, uniform requests → Batch higher; MoE gets more efficient on throughput per dollar than at small batch.
  • Is dense 47B comparable? → Compute-wise the MoE is ~3.6x cheaper per token; memory is the same.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team approved an MoE migration on the basis of "13B active," then discovered the multi-GPU requirement only after procurement. A one-page memory and concurrency model would have flagged it in an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes it fits.
  • Hire: computes weights and KV, shards across GPUs.
  • Strong hire: adds Little's-law concurrency, bandwidth caveat at high batch, quantization and eval plan.

questions.promptHtml: You are asked to serve a large MoE model in production. What is different from serving a dense model of the same active size? Cover parallelism, batching, latency and failure modes.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who read the blog from people who have thought about distributed inference.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Three differences. Memory: all experts must be resident, so the model needs multi-GPU sharding even though the compute is small. Communication: with expert parallelism each GPU holds a subset of experts, so tokens must be sent to the GPUs hosting their chosen experts and back, an all-to-all per MoE layer, which becomes the bottleneck on slow interconnects. Load imbalance: routing is data-dependent, so a hot expert makes one GPU the straggler and sets the step latency. Batching helps utilization because more tokens means every expert has work, but small batches waste bandwidth by reading experts that few tokens use."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Parallelism options: tensor parallel (split each matrix across GPUs; all-reduce per layer), expert parallel (distribute experts; all-to-all per MoE layer for dispatch and combine), data parallel for attention layers with EP for experts (the pattern used in large DeepSeek-style deployments; verify specifics), pipeline parallel across layers.
  • Decode regime: for one sequence with top-2 of 8, only 2 experts are read, a bandwidth win. At batch B, expected distinct experts touched is about E (1 - (1 - k/E)^B): with E=8, k=2, B=8, 8 x (1 - 0.75^8) = 7.2 experts, so a modest batch already reads nearly every expert. So the "13B speed" claim holds mostly at tiny batches.
  • Prefill: many tokens per expert, compute-bound, more efficient.
  • Tail latency: step time = slowest GPU. Imbalance factor matters. Mitigations: replicate hot experts, capacity-aware or load-aware placement, careful batching.
  • Failure modes: one GPU down takes out its experts (whole replica); capacity dropping behavior differences between training and inference stacks; numerical differences between kernels causing routing flips on near-tied logits (so subtle nondeterminism).
  • Interconnect: NVLink within a node is fast; cross-node all-to-all over network can dominate, so keep an EP group inside a node when possible.
token -> router -> GPU3(expert 5) --all-to-all--> compute --all-to-all--> combine
step latency ~ max over GPUs (compute_i) + 2 * all-to-all time per MoE layer

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(expected distinct experts touched)

def distinct_experts(E, k, B):
    return E * (1 - (1 - k / E) ** B)

for B in (1, 4, 8, 32):
    print(B, round(distinct_experts(8, 2, B), 2))   # 2.0, 5.47, 7.2, 8.0 (approx)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating throughput as proportional to active params regardless of batch.
  • Ignoring interconnect: a great model on PCIe-only boxes can be slower than expected.
  • Forgetting that one replica needs all GPUs of its group healthy.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. TP vs EP for MoE? → TP splits every expert thinly with all-reduces; EP keeps experts whole but needs all-to-all and suffers imbalance. Choice depends on interconnect and batch.
  2. How would you detect a hot expert in prod? → Per-expert token counts and per-GPU step times from the engine's metrics; compare p99 to mean.
  3. How do you capacity plan? → Load test with your own traffic mix since routing is content dependent; do not use synthetic uniform prompts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "needs more GPUs." Senior: all-to-all cost, batch-dependent bandwidth, straggler effect, interconnect topology, and load testing on real content.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Benchmarks on synthetic random prompts showed balanced routing; real code-heavy traffic skewed to a few experts and p99 latency doubled.

questions.contextHtml:
You port a top-2 MoE layer from a reference implementation. Offline tests pass on shapes, but compared with reference outputs on 1,000 prompts the ported model has mean logit difference of 0.8 and perplexity rises from 6.1 to 7.4. Training-time load-balancing loss is not involved (inference only). Code:

def route(x, router, k=2):
    probs = torch.softmax(router(x), dim=-1)      # (T, E)
    topv, topi = probs.topk(k, dim=-1)
    return topv, topi                             # used directly as combine weights

def forward(x, router, experts):
    w, idx = route(x, router)
    out = torch.zeros_like(x)
    for s in range(2):
        for e in range(len(experts)):
            m = idx[:, s] == e
            out[m] += w[m, s, None] * experts[e](x[m])
    return out

Distractors: the team suspects bf16 precision, a tokenizer difference, or FlashAttention versions.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and explain how you would prove it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames precision and lowers dtype to fp32, or rewrites the loop, never noticing the weights do not sum to 1.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which reference defines the gating (softmax over all experts then renormalize, or softmax over selected logits)? Do weights in the checkpoint expect normalized weights? Any shared experts?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin to the reference implementation for production; keep the port in staging.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Missing renormalization of top-k weights; (b) wrong expert ordering/indexing; (c) bf16; (d) tokenizer; (e) attention kernel.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layer-by-layer diff against the reference with hooks: compare the first MoE layer output on one token. Print topv.sum(-1): with 8 experts the top-2 softmax mass is often 0.4 to 0.8, not 1. That already differs from the reference's weights summing to 1. Dtype and tokenizer ruled out by identical input ids and fp32 run that still disagrees.
  5. Root cause: The model was trained with softmax over only the selected top-k logits, so combine weights sum to 1. Softmax over all E then top-k gives weights with sum less than 1, shrinking every MoE layer's output by a data-dependent factor, and the error compounds over 32 layers.
  6. Fix:
topv, topi = router(x).topk(k, dim=-1)      # logits
w = torch.softmax(topv, dim=-1)              # normalize over selected only

(Some architectures instead use all-expert softmax then renormalize; follow the checkpoint's reference. Do not guess.) 7. Prevention: Golden-output test per layer against the reference on fixed inputs with a tolerance; assert w.sum(-1) ~ 1 in the router unit test; compare perplexity on a fixed set in CI. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not tune precision flags before localizing the first divergent layer; bisecting by layer is cheap and decisive.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ties near the top-k boundary → Tiny numerical differences flip routing, so exact bitwise parity across kernels is unrealistic; use tolerances on logits and perplexity.
  • Token dropping at inference → Check the reference sets no capacity limit; adding one causes silent quality loss.
  • Shared expert present → Its output is added outside the routed weights; make sure it is not normalized into them.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A port looked fine on loss for short prompts and failed on long ones; the cause was a gating normalization difference that only compounded noticeably over deep stacks. A per-layer golden test found it in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames dtype.
  • Hire: spots missing renormalization.
  • Strong hire: bisects layer-wise, adds tests, notes ties/capacity nuances.

questions.promptHtml: Explain knowledge distillation for LLMs. What are the variants, what does a student actually learn, and when is distillation the right architecture decision?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can reason about trading a large teacher for a deployable student, including the legal and quality limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Distillation trains a small student to imitate a large teacher. Classic logit distillation minimizes KL divergence between the student's and teacher's token distributions, which carries more signal than one-hot labels because the teacher's soft probabilities encode which wrong answers are nearly right. For LLMs the common practical version is sequence-level: generate outputs, including reasoning traces, from the teacher and SFT the student on them. DeepSeek did this at scale, distilling R1 reasoning traces into 1.5B to 70B models. It is right when I have a narrow, high-volume task and a strong teacher; it is wrong when the student lacks the capacity or when the teacher's license forbids it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Logit (white-box) distillation: loss = alpha x KL(p_teacher^T || p_student^T) + (1 - alpha) x CE(labels), with temperature T softening distributions. Requires teacher logits and a shared tokenizer/vocab (or an alignment trick), which limits you to open teachers.
  • Sequence-level (black-box): sample teacher outputs for a prompt set, filter them (verifier, judge, tests, dedupe), then SFT. Works with API teachers, needs no logits. The student learns the teacher's style and reasoning patterns, but not its full knowledge.
  • On-policy distillation variants: student generates, teacher scores its tokens; reduces train/test mismatch (concept only).
  • What transfers: format, style, task skill, reasoning patterns. What doesn't: broad world knowledge beyond the student's capacity, long-tail facts; students can learn to sound confident and still be wrong.
  • Data is the lever: coverage of the real input distribution, difficulty mix, filtering for correctness (reject teacher mistakes), and held-out eval on real traffic.
  • Constraints: provider terms of service may forbid training competing models on outputs (check each provider's terms, verify); output licenses on open models vary.
  • Related: distillation vs quantization vs pruning: distillation changes the model (new weights, new capacity), quantization changes precision only.
Teacher (70B) --generate+filter--> 200k (prompt, response) pairs --SFT--> Student (8B)
Teacher logits (open weights) --KL loss--> Student            [logit distillation]

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(logit distillation loss)

import torch.nn.functional as F

def distill_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, labels, T=2.0, alpha=0.5):
    kd = F.kl_div(F.log_softmax(student_logits / T, dim=-1),
                  F.softmax(teacher_logits / T, dim=-1),
                  reduction="batchmean") * (T * T)
    ce = F.cross_entropy(student_logits.view(-1, student_logits.size(-1)),
                         labels.view(-1), ignore_index=-100)
    return alpha * kd + (1 - alpha) * ce

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Training on unfiltered teacher outputs: the student inherits teacher errors with confidence.
  • Evaluating on the same distribution as the distillation prompts, hiding overfitting.
  • Ignoring license or ToS limits on using outputs.
  • Expecting a 1B student to match a 70B teacher on open-ended reasoning.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why multiply KL by T^2? → Soft-target gradients scale as 1/T^2; the factor keeps their magnitude comparable to the hard-label loss.
  2. How do you know the student is good enough? → Held-out evals on real traffic by slice, plus a regression suite of teacher-vs-student disagreements reviewed by humans.
  3. When is RL better than distillation for a small model? → When no strong teacher exists but you have a verifiable reward; distillation from a stronger reasoning teacher is usually cheaper and more effective for small models (the R1 paper reports this; verify the exact comparison).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "small model learns from big model." Senior: logit vs sequence-level, filtering, license risk, capacity ceilings and an eval design that catches distribution shift.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A distilled 8B served the 90% easy traffic at a fraction of the cost, with a router escalating hard prompts to the teacher; the filtering step caught 6% wrong teacher answers that would otherwise have been learned.

questions.contextHtml: A coding assistant moved from a standard chat model to a reasoning model after a quality push. Traffic: 400k requests/day. Before: average 900 input tokens and 350 output tokens, p95 latency 4 s. After: average 900 input, 350 visible output plus 3,800 reasoning tokens, p95 latency 38 s. Illustrative prices: $3 per 1M input, $15 per 1M output tokens for both (verify real pricing; reasoning tokens bill as output on most providers). Pass@1 on the internal eval rose from 61% to 74% overall, but on the 55% of traffic classified as "simple edits and explanations" it rose only from 93% to 94%. Support tickets about "slow responses" tripled; the CFO asks for a 40% cost cut.
questions.promptHtml: How do you diagnose and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reduce max tokens" or "switch back"; both ignore that the gain is concentrated in hard queries.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the quality/latency SLO per request type? Can the UX stream partial output or show progress? Is thinking effort adjustable on this provider? Which segments drive the 74% vs 61% gap?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap the thinking budget or lower the effort setting for the interactive path, add timeouts and a progress indicator; keep the model but protect p95.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Most traffic is easy, so thinking tokens are mostly waste; (b) a few prompt patterns trigger very long chains (loops, ambiguous requests); (c) legacy prompts with "think step by step" or long few-shot examples add redundant reasoning; (d) retries duplicate spend.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log reasoning tokens per request by segment; histogram and p99 (find the long tail); join with eval outcomes; sample top-1% longest traces; check prompt templates.
  5. Root cause: Cost per request before: 900 x $3/1M + 350 x $15/1M = $0.0027 + $0.00525 = $0.00795. After: output = 4,150 tokens x $15/1M = $0.06225 + $0.0027 = $0.06495, about 8.2x. Daily: 400k x $0.00795 = $3.2k before vs 400k x $0.065 = $26k after. Latency scales with generated tokens: roughly 4,150 vs 350.
  6. Fix: Short-term: route by difficulty. A cheap classifier (or the cheap model with a confidence signal) sends the 55% simple traffic to the non-reasoning model and the rest to the reasoning model with an effort cap. Estimated: 0.55 x $0.00795 + 0.45 x $0.065 = $0.0336 per request, about $13.4k/day, about 48% below $26k. Quality estimated as 0.55 x 93% + 0.45 x (hard-segment score, to be measured) which preserves most of the 13-point gain. Long-term: tune effort per segment, cache repeated queries, stream partial output.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards for reasoning tokens per request and per segment, per-feature budget alerts, an eval that reports quality per cost.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not cap thinking globally with a tiny limit: hard problems then fail silently and the quality gain disappears. I would not remove reasoning for everyone because the headline gain came from the hard half.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Router misroutes 10% of hard queries as simple → Use fallback on validator failure (tests fail) and measure routed accuracy; bias the router toward the reasoning side for costly errors.
  • Provider hides reasoning tokens → You still see counts in usage metadata; you cannot inspect traces, so rely on usage and outcomes.
  • Latency still too high for hard queries → Stream a status, run async, or use a smaller reasoning model plus verifier.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team celebrated an eval jump and shipped, then discovered 70% of spend was reasoning tokens on trivial prompts. A difficulty router recovered most of the cost within a sprint while keeping the hard-segment gains.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cap tokens or revert.
  • Hire: computes cost, segments traffic, adds routing.
  • Strong hire: quantifies blended cost and quality, handles misrouting fallback, monitors per-segment reasoning tokens.

questions.contextHtml: A claims app lets users upload photos of damage and asks a hosted vision-language model to describe them. Last week the median upload was a 1024x768 phone photo costing about 800 image tokens. After a mobile release that sends original 12 MP photos (4032x3024), logs show: prompt_tokens=6,412 per request (up from ~1,000), p95 latency 3 s to 9 s, and the daily bill up 5x. Quality on a spot check is unchanged. The model tiling behavior is vendor-defined (illustrative: images are split into 512px tiles at 170 tokens each plus a base of 85, with large images downscaled so the short side is at most 768px before tiling; verify the actual provider's documentation).
questions.promptHtml: Explain the spike and what you would do.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The model got slower" or "compress the JPEG", which does not change pixel dimensions or the tile count.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the provider documentation say about image tokenization and detail modes? Which release changed? Does the task need fine detail (reading serial numbers)? Are images ever multi-image per request?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Resize to a bounded long edge on the server (or roll back the client) before the model call; set a low-detail option if the provider offers one.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Image dimensions changed, so tile count changed; (b) a bug attaches the same image multiple times; (c) text prompt grew; (d) retry storm. Latency rise from more prefill tokens.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare prompt_tokens with image width/height in logs; replay one old and one new image through the provider's token-count endpoint or documented formula; check message payload for duplicates.
  5. Root cause: Image tokens depend on resolution (in tile-based schemes) not on file size. 4032x3024 produces many more tiles than 1024x768, and prefill cost grows with tokens. With the stated illustrative scheme: after downscale the image yields about 1024x768 (short side 768) which is 2x2 = 4 tiles x 170 + 85 = 765 tokens, whereas 6,412 implies something else (e.g., a different scheme or high-detail multi-tile). Hence I would not trust my formula: measure actual tokens per resolution, with the vendor's counter.
  6. Fix: Short-term: normalize to a max long edge (for example 1,568 or what the provider's guidance recommends; verify) server-side; Long-term: a preprocessing service that picks resolution by task (full detail only on request), caches results by image hash, and logs image tokens separately.
  7. Prevention: Alert on prompt tokens per request, a contract test for max image dimension in the API, per-feature cost dashboard split into text vs image tokens.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not apply the same downscale to OCR-type tasks without testing; small text becomes unreadable. I would not rely on JPEG quality reduction for token cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Some claims need reading a VIN plate → Two-pass: low-res overview, then a cropped high-res region on demand.
  • Users upload 10 images per claim → Cap per-claim image count or batch asynchronously.
  • Vendor changes tiling in a model update → Our token counter must call the vendor's counting API or be validated in CI.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A release "improved photo fidelity" and quadrupled spend overnight, because nobody connected pixel dimensions to token count. A resize step and an alert on tokens per request fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the model or compresses files.
  • Hire: ties cost to resolution and tiles, resizes server-side.
  • Strong hire: measures with vendor tooling instead of trusting a formula, adds alerts, handles detail-critical tasks.

questions.contextHtml: A document-extraction product calls a large model (illustrative: $5 per 1M input, $15 per 1M output) for 2M invoices/month: 3,000 input and 400 output tokens each, about $42k/month. Field-level accuracy is 96.5% with p95 of 6 s. The team distilled a 8B student from 150k teacher-labeled invoices (teacher outputs, not human-verified). Offline on a held-out set the student scores 95.8%. Shadow traffic for a week shows 95.9% agreement-adjusted accuracy, but customer C (about 4% of volume, many scanned multi-language invoices) shows 88%. Product wants to cut over this month.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Flip traffic based on the 95.8% average; ignores the slice failure and the fact the labels came from the teacher.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "accuracy" mean when labels come from the teacher (agreement, not truth)? What is the cost of errors per field (payments)? Can we sample human labels? Is customer C's drop a data or language issue?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Nothing is broken yet; keep the teacher as the production path. Define the cutover gate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The training set underrepresents scanned and multi-language invoices; (b) OCR/layout inputs differ for scans; (c) student capacity on non-English; (d) teacher labels wrong on that slice, so the student learned mistakes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Slice metrics by customer, language, scan quality; human-label 500 samples from customer C and score both models vs truth; compare the training distribution to production.
  5. Root cause: Distribution gap between teacher-labeled training data and the long-tail slice; teacher-agreement metrics overstate quality.
  6. Fix: Add targeted data for the weak slice (teacher plus human-checked labels), retrain; use confidence plus validation rules (totals sum, date formats) to escalate uncertain docs to the teacher. Cost projection: student traffic cost maybe 10 to 15 times lower (verify by benchmark); if 80% handled by the student and 20% escalated, blended cost about 0.2 x $42k + 0.8 x $4.2k = $8.4k + $3.4k = about $11.8k/month, roughly a 72% cut (assumes the student costs about a tenth per call).
  7. Prevention: Gated rollout: 1% to 5% to 25% to 100% with automated rollback on slice metrics; monthly human-labeled audit; drift monitors; keep a teacher-shadow sample (1 to 2%).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not cut over customer C until its human-evaluated accuracy meets the contract. I would not retire the teacher; it is the fallback and the label source for future retrains.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Teacher model is deprecated by the vendor → Freeze a labeled corpus now; retrain with the successor and re-validate against humans.
  • Escalation rate is 35%, not 20% → Savings drop to about 0.35 x 42k + 0.65 x 4k = $17.3k; tune thresholds, then target the failure slice with data.
  • Contract requires 97% → Neither model meets it alone; use validators and human review for flagged fields.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A distilled model matched the teacher in aggregate and silently failed on one enterprise client's scans for a month; the account owner found it, not the metrics. Slice dashboards were added to the cutover checklist afterward.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cuts over on average accuracy.
  • Hire: slices, human-labels, and escalation fallback.
  • Strong hire: staged rollout with rollback gates, cost projections under different escalation rates, and a retrain/deprecation plan.

questions.promptHtml: Besides a model that thinks in a long chain of thought, what other ways can you spend extra inference compute to improve answer quality? What are the trade-offs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks breadth on inference-time scaling and the discipline of tying techniques to verifiers and cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The main families are parallel and sequential. Parallel: sample N answers and pick one, by majority vote (self-consistency), by a reward model or verifier (best-of-N), or by running tests for code. Sequential: let the model revise, critique and retry using feedback, or use a longer thinking budget. Parallel methods need a way to choose; they work best when a cheap, reliable verifier exists, like unit tests or exact-match math answers. Cost scales roughly linearly with N, while quality gains flatten, so I tune N against the verifier's accuracy and the latency budget."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Self-consistency: sample N chains at temperature above 0, extract final answers, take the mode. Works when answers are short and comparable (math, classification); useless for free-form text unless you can canonicalize.
  • Best-of-N with a verifier: if the verifier is imperfect, increasing N can select adversarial or reward-hacked samples, so gains plateau or reverse (reward over-optimization).
  • Sequential refinement: generate, test, feed back error, regenerate (a loop common in coding agents; see the agents track). Needs reliable feedback; self-critique without external signal gives modest or negative gains on many tasks.
  • Search over reasoning steps (tree search with process rewards): research-level, high complexity, rarely worth it in products.
  • Latency: parallel samples are concurrent so wall-clock is roughly one generation if you have capacity, but cost and throughput usage multiply by N; sequential adds wall-clock.
  • Rule of thumb for the math: if one sample is right with probability p and a perfect verifier exists, P(at least one right in N) = 1 - (1 - p)^N: p=0.4, N=5 gives 1 - 0.6^5 = 0.92. A noisy verifier erodes that.
prompt -> [sample 1][sample 2]...[sample N] -> verifier / vote -> answer     (parallel)
prompt -> draft -> check/test -> feedback -> revise -> ...                    (sequential)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from collections import Counter

def self_consistency(sample_fn, extract_fn, n=7):
    answers = [extract_fn(sample_fn()) for _ in range(n)]
    answers = [a for a in answers if a is not None]
    return Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0][0] if answers else None

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Majority voting on free-text outputs.
  • Using the same model as both generator and judge and expecting independent errors.
  • Not setting temperature above 0 for diversity (identical samples).
  • Ignoring that N-way sampling multiplies the bill.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is a verifier trustworthy? → Programmatic checks (tests, schema, exact answer, constraint solvers) are; LLM judges are noisy and biased.
  2. Does best-of-N always improve with N? → No: noisy verifiers lead to over-optimization; measure N against held-out truth.
  3. How do you pick between a long-thinking model and best-of-N? → Compare quality per dollar and per second on your task; a reasoning model is a single call to manage, best-of-N gives control and parallelism.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "sample multiple times and vote." Senior: parallel vs sequential, verifier quality as the limiter, 1-(1-p)^N math, and cost/latency accounting.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A code-fix feature got a bigger quality gain from running generated patches against the existing unit tests (best-of-4) than from upgrading the model, at lower cost.

questions.contextHtml: A procurement team asks: "Use the new multimodal model so we can just send PDFs and get structured line items." Volume: 50k PDFs/month, 5 to 40 pages each (median 12), mix of digital-native and scanned, 15% with dense tables; they need totals reconciled to the cent and an audit trail. A vision call for a page costs roughly 1,200 image tokens (illustrative); the same page extracted as text is about 600 text tokens. The vendor pitches the multimodal path as "no OCR pipeline needed." There is no labeled dataset yet.
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend, and how do you handle the ambiguity?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts "just use the multimodal model" or insists on a custom OCR pipeline without evidence on either side.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the required field accuracy and the penalty for an error (payments)? Do we need bounding-box citations for audit? Is data allowed to leave our environment? How fast must results be (batch overnight vs interactive)? How many distinct vendor layouts?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; start by building a labeled set of about 300 documents stratified by native/scanned, tables, layout, language, then compare approaches on it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) For digital-native PDFs, text-layer extraction plus a text LLM is cheaper and exact; (b) for scans and complex tables, a VLM or layout-aware OCR does better; (c) a hybrid (route by document type) wins overall; (d) pure VLM fails on dense numeric tables and long documents through dropped rows.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run three pipelines on the labeled set: text-layer + LLM, OCR/layout + LLM, VLM direct. Score field-level accuracy, row recall in tables, reconciliation pass rate (sum of lines equals total), cost per document, p95 latency.
  5. Root cause: The ambiguity is in the requirement ("just send PDFs"). The architecture choice depends on document type and error cost, not on which model is newest.
  6. Fix (recommendation): Hybrid with validators: extract text layer when present; use the VLM on scanned pages and table regions; arithmetic validation (line items sum to total, tax math) triggers re-extraction or human review. Cost sketch for the median 12-page doc: all-VLM 12 x 1,200 = 14,400 input tokens; text path 12 x 600 = 7,200 plus VLM only on about 30% of pages, roughly 7,200 + 3.6 x 1,200 = 11,520 tokens, with higher precision on digital pages. Compute in dollars from real prices.
  7. Prevention: Per-field confidence and citations to page regions, drift monitoring on new vendors/layouts, weekly sampled human audit, versioned prompts and models.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not promise "no pipeline needed": validators, retries, and review UI are the pipeline. I would not process 40-page PDFs in a single call without chunking; long multimodal contexts increase dropped-row errors and cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Data cannot leave the VPC → Open-weight VLM or OCR self-hosted; accept an eval re-run and probable accuracy gap.
  • Accuracy needed is 99.9% → Human-in-the-loop for flagged fields, with automation targeting 90 to 95% touchless, not 100%.
  • Vendor updates the VLM monthly → Pin model versions and run the golden set on each upgrade.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team shipped a direct-VLM extractor that read digits nicely but dropped a row in long tables about 2% of the time; totals did not reconcile. A simple sum check caught it, and the fix was cropping tables and extracting per region.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts vendor claim or picks by taste.
  • Hire: proposes comparison on a labeled set and notes digital vs scanned.
  • Strong hire: hybrid routing, arithmetic validators, cost math, audit trail and governance, plus explicit handling of the ambiguous requirement.
